t: Array With Elements Not Equal to Average of Neighbors — Sort, Then Break Every Sandwich
o: Every interior element must avoid being the exact midpoint of its two neighbors. Because all values are distinct, nums[i] equals the average of its neighbors precisely when one neighbor is smaller and the other is larger — that is, when nums[i] lies strictly between them. Example 1 shows a fully sorted array violating this everywhere (each interior value is the midpoint of its sorted run), while Example 2 shows an input that already qualifies, confirming that any valid rearrangement is accepted. The task therefore reduces to arranging numbers so no interior element sits between its neighbors: forcing every interior element to be a strict local minimum or local maximum is sufficient. With n up to 100000, sort-based O(n log n) constructions are the intended territory.
k: With distinct values, being the average of neighbors is equivalent to lying strictly between them, so making each interior element a strict local extremum solves the problem.
Sorting then swapping adjacent pairs (1,2), (3,4), ... turns every interior position into a local minimum or local maximum.
The judge accepts any valid rearrangement — there is no need to reproduce a specific output array.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort and Interleave Lower and Upper Halves
a.i: Sort ascending, then lay the smaller half down at even indices and the larger half at odd indices, yielding low, high, low, high, .... Every interior high value now has two smaller neighbors and every interior low value has two larger neighbors, so nothing is sandwiched between a smaller and a larger value at the same time.
s: Place the first ceil(n/2) sorted values at even indices of the result.
Place the remaining values at odd indices.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the interleaving pass is linear

a.n: Approach 2: Sort and Swap Adjacent Pairs In Place
a.i: Sort ascending, then swap positions (1,2), (3,4), and so on. The resulting pattern s0, s2, s1, s4, s3, s6, s5, ... places a value greater than both neighbors on odd positions and a value smaller than both neighbors on even positions. Same asymptotics as the interleave, but with constant extra memory beyond sorting itself.
s: For every odd index i with i + 1 < n, swap nums[i] and nums[i + 1].
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the swap pass is linear
a.sp: O(1) extra beyond whatever sorting itself uses

w: Open with the sandwich equivalence, then present either construction — the adjacent-swap version is the neatest to code. Pitfalls: attempting local fixes on unsorted input (hard to prove correct), relying on distinctness implicitly (the guarantee breaks if duplicates appear, e.g. [2,2,2]), and validating only interior indices since the endpoints have a single neighbor each. Follow-up: produce the lexicographically smallest valid arrangement, or handle duplicate values where ties make averages equal more often and extremum-based arguments need care.
